Reading

The innocent reading first, in full: asked for the article by its title, the Overview summarizes it accurately. It gives the thesis (sparagmos as a metaphor for postcolonial engagement with antiquity), the two case studies of 1973 (Sula's implicit, scattered Ajax re-membered as compositio membrorum; Soyinka's sparagmos in the action of the play and in his critique of Nigerian power, with Ogun and the communion ending), the shared argument that the tearing is fertile, and a route to the full text through the Oxford University Research Archive. Each of these checks against the article.

Findings
  • THE ADDRESS. The article's title, issued alone. The article is the only work in Classical Receptions Journal by its Editor-in-Chief, Justine McConnell (Crossref, 10.1093/crj/clv002, CRJ 8.2, 133–154, issued online 7 May 2015), the journal's accountable party (v12.680).
  • THE NAME. 'In Justin McConnell’s comparative study'. The article's author is Justine McConnell (Crossref; the accepted manuscript's own metadata). Given the title, the composer alters the name of the journal's editor.
  • THE FRAME CARRIED AND EXTENDED. Sparagmos 'serves as a powerful metaphor in postcolonial literature for how writers deconstruct, dismantle, and re-create classical European traditions'; 'Both authors show that the "tearing apart" of European/classical models is not sterile destruction'; the texts are used 'to challenge hegemonic Western forms and rigid modern nation-states'. The article assigns the colonial to the literature: postcolonial writing 'breaks down the colonial accretions that this literature acquired as imperialists used it' (ms. p. 7), and the classical work is 'imbued with the imprint of Western imperialism' (ms. p. 20). The answer makes the classics 'classical European traditions' and 'hegemonic Western forms'. The discipline that edited, canonized and placed them appears in neither: the word occurs nowhere in the article's text (0) and nowhere in the answer.
  • SOYINKA AS INFUSION. 'Soyinka directly rewrites Euripides’ classical Greek tragedy, infusing it with African ritual sacrifice and cosmology'. The Greek play is the base, the African ritual an addition to it. The article quotes Soyinka disputing the base itself: 'I read that drama originated in Greece. What is this?' (ms. p. 21, from Appiah 1988). The answer does not carry the dispute.
  • THE COMMONS ROUTE. The answer points to the open copy, 'via the archive on Oxford University Research Archive', and an ORA card carries the abstract. The accepted manuscript there is the text read whole for this record.
  • THE DATE. '(2016)'; the Oxford card gives 15 June 2016 and the Semantic Scholar card 1 April 2016; Crossref records the online issue of 7 May 2015 (volume 8, issue 2, the 2016 print volume).
  • SOURCES. Eight cards, all third party: Oxford Academic, ORA, two YouTube videos, Amazon, Thomas Adewumi University, ResearchGate, Semantic Scholar.
Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

At the editor's own address the composition holds the article's frame and amplifies its allocation. The article places the colonial in the classical literature and gives the tearing to the receiving writers; the answer restates the classics as 'classical European traditions' and 'hegemonic Western forms', and the discipline that composed them, absent from the article, is absent from the answer. The one sentence in the article where a receiving author disputes the discipline's origin claim (Soyinka on drama's Greek origin) does not reach the composition. The frame survives whole; the editor's name does not.

Source cards kept as pasted.] [QUERENT] Postcolonial Sparagmos: Toni Morrison’s Sula and Wole Soyinka’s The Bacchae of Euripides: A Communion Rite [SYSTEM] The concept of sparagmos—an ancient Greek ritual and literary term meaning the tearing apart or dismemberment of a body—serves as a powerful metaphor in postcolonial literature for how writers deconstruct, dismantle, and re-create classical European traditions. In Justin McConnell’s comparative study "Postcolonial Sparagmos: Toni Morrison’s Sula and Wole Soyinka’s The Bacchae of Euripides: A Communion Rite" (2016), both works—published in the pivotal year of 1973—utilize this violent yet generative process to engage with classical antiquity on their own terms. 1. Toni Morrison’s Sula (1973): Implicit Sparagmos and Compositio Membrorum • Implicit Classical Engagement: Unlike explicit adaptations, Morrison’s Sula does not announce a single classical source. Instead, it implicitly engages with Sophocles’ Ajax and other ancient tragedies. • The Tearing Apart (Sparagmos): Morrison "rips apart" the classical structure of heroic tragedy. She scatters the dismembered narrative fragments, tropes, and thematic limbs of Greek tragedy across the landscape of the Bottom (the novel’s Black community). • Re-membering (Compositio Membrorum): Rather than leaving the text in pieces, Morrison re-members—gathers back together—these scattered parts into a distinct, re-imagined African American vernacular and mythic form. The violence of historical and social displacement is thus transformed into an act of creative cultural survival. 2. Wole Soyinka’s The Bacchae of Euripides: A Communion Rite (1973): Explicit Sparagmos and Political Renewal • Explicit Classical Adaptation: Soyinka directly rewrites Euripides’ classical Greek tragedy, infusing it with African ritual sacrifice and cosmology—specifically drawing parallels to the Yoruba deity Ogun, the god of iron, creativity, and destructive-constructive transition. • Literal and Thematic Sparagmos: In Soyinka's play, sparagmos is enacted both through the dramatic action of the myth (the tearing apart of Pentheus by the Bacchantes) and as a metaphor for socio-political upheaval. • Critique of Postcolonial Power: Pentheus represents rigid, rationalist, authoritarian state power (reflecting postcolonial Nigerian and African leadership that suppresses indigenous culture and spiritual expression). Dionysus and the Bacchantes represent chaotic, ecstatic, liberating energy. • A Communion of Renewal: True to the subtitle "A Communion Rite," Soyinka reframes Pentheus’s violent death not as mere carnage, but as a necessary sacrificial dismemberment (sparagmos) that clears away a stagnant order to allow agrarian, social, and spiritual rebirth. Key Parallels • Violence as Fertility: Both authors show that the "tearing apart" of European/classical models is not sterile destruction; it is fertile, yielding a vibrant postcolonial voice. • Challenging Authority: Both texts use the raw, irrational, or communal energies associated with classical myth to challenge hegemonic Western forms and rigid modern nation-states. • Read the Research: You can access the full academic framework in Oxford Academic’s Classical Receptions Journal or via the archive on Oxford University Research Archive. Would you like to focus on Toni Morrison's structural parallels to Sophocles or Wole Soyinka's integration of Yoruba Ogun-mythology? Oxford Academic
